title: Music Fundamentals I: Pitch, Major Scales and Key Signatures, Rhythm, Meter

guide.summary: Unit 1 covers the building blocks of notation: pitch and clefs, major scales and key signatures, the circle of fifths, scale-degree names, rhythm, simple and compound meter, and basic expressive terms.

sections.heading: Pitch and clefs
sections.body: Pitches are named A–G and labeled by octave (C4 = middle C). The treble clef circles G4; the bass clef's dots surround F3; the alto clef centers middle C on the middle line (viola), and the tenor clef places middle C on the fourth line (cello, bassoon, trombone in high registers). Accidentals raise or lower pitches by a half step (sharp, flat) or cancel (natural). Enharmonic equivalents sound the same but are spelled differently (F♯ = G♭).

sections.heading: Major scales and keys
sections.body: A major scale follows whole and half steps W–W–H–W–W–W–H. Scale-degree names: 1 tonic, 2 supertonic, 3 mediant, 4 subdominant, 5 dominant, 6 submediant, 7 leading tone (a half step below the tonic). Sharps appear in the order F C G D A E B, flats in the order B E A D G C F. With sharps, the major key is a half step above the last sharp; with flats, it is the next-to-last flat (F major has one flat). The circle of fifths arranges keys by adding one sharp per fifth up and one flat per fifth down; keys a fifth apart share all but one pitch.

sections.heading: Rhythm and meter
sections.body: In simple meters, the beat divides into two (2/4, 3/4, 4/4, 2/2); in compound meters, the beat is a dotted note that divides into three (6/8 = two dotted-quarter beats, 9/8 = three, 12/8 = four). Meters are duple, triple, or quadruple by beats per measure. Syncopation stresses weak beats or offbeats; hemiola temporarily regroups beats, for example two bars of 3/4 heard as three groups of two. Ties extend durations across beats; dots add half the note's value. Expressive terms include tempo markings (largo, adagio, andante, moderato, allegro, presto), dynamics (pp to ff, crescendo, decrescendo), and articulations (staccato, legato, accent).

sections.heading: Worked example: identifying keys
sections.body: To find the major key from a signature with sharps, take the last sharp and go up a half step: with F♯, C♯, and G♯, the key is A major. With flats, the next-to-last flat names the key: with B♭, E♭, and A♭, the key is E♭ major. One flat is F major. Each major key shares its signature with a relative minor a minor third below: A major with F♯ minor, E♭ major with C minor. In dictation and sight-singing, identify the key first, then think in scale degrees, which makes melodies easier to hear and notate.

sections.heading: Rhythm practice
sections.body: In simple meter, count beats and divisions with numbers and 'and' (1 & 2 &); in compound meter, divide each beat into three (1 la li 2 la li). Watch for dotted rhythms, ties across beats, and syncopation. When writing rhythms, beam notes to show the beat, especially in compound meter, where eighth notes are grouped in threes. On aural questions, tap the beat while listening to decide whether the meter is duple, triple, or quadruple, and whether beats divide in two or three.

sections.heading: Aural skills tips
sections.body: Practice singing major scales with solfège (do re mi fa sol la ti do) or numbers, and identify scale degrees by their tendencies: ti pulls up to do, fa pulls down to mi. Recognizing these tendencies helps with dictation. Listen for the tonic at the beginning and end of phrases.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students confuse 6/8 with 3/4, misread clefs, and forget accidentals that carry through a measure. Double-check key signatures before writing scales.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know pitch, octave, clef, ledger line, accidental, enharmonic, scale degree, key signature, circle of fifths, meter, beat, division, syncopation, hemiola, tempo, and dynamics.

sections.heading: Practice routine
sections.body: Spend ten minutes a day on fundamentals: name notes in treble and bass clef, write key signatures from memory, and clap rhythms in simple and compound meter. Use flashcards or an online drill until you can identify any key signature in a few seconds.

keyTakeaways: Order of sharps FCGDAEB; flats BEADGCF.
Simple beats divide in 2; compound in 3.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the last sharp rule (key is a half step above).
Confusing leading tone and subtonic (in natural minor).
examTips: Count beats, not just notes, in compound meter.

**Scale:** W W H W W W H · **Degrees:** tonic, supertonic, mediant, subdominant, dominant, submediant, leading tone

**Sharps:** F C G D A E B · **Flats:** B E A D G C F

**Meter:** simple (beat ÷ 2) vs compound (dotted beat ÷ 3) · duple/triple/quadruple

**Clefs:** treble G4 · bass F3 · alto C4 middle line · tenor C4 4th line

**Tempo:** largo < adagio < andante < moderato < allegro < presto

rubric.description: E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C D E♭.

practice.sampleResponse:
a. A major: F♯, C♯, G♯.
b. The relative minor of A major is F♯ minor.
c. E♭ major: E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C D E♭.
d. 9/8 is compound triple: three dotted-quarter beats, each dividing into three eighths.
e. C♯ is enharmonic with D♭.
f. The leading tone of B♭ major is A.
